channel.title: Los Angeles Review of Books – Reviews
channel.description: Book reviews from the Los Angeles Review of Books.

item.title: Murky Effects
item.description: A novel of desire and domestic disorder amid a disintegrating literary establishment.

item.title: Mourning, Melancholy—or Ta’zieh
item.description: Visiting Azadeh Akhlaghi at the Peabody Museum.

item.title: Endlessly Reproducible Originality
item.description: Sam Riviere’s new novel suggests that, in a literary culture already organized around copying, the machines may prove better at being writers than we are.

item.title: No Woman, No Cry
item.description: Libyan author Mohammed Alnaas’s ‘Bread on Uncle Milad’s Table’ is a tale of masculinity and vulnerability.

item.title: Learning How to Travel from the Ancients
item.description: M. D. Usher assembles an anthology of ancient travel writing refitted for our age of global tourism.

item.title: California Sons: Miriam Pawel’s “The Browns of California”
item.description: Jake Wertz reviews “The Browns of California,” a four-generation biography of the Brown family and a portrait of the state they shaped.

item.title: Love, Sickness
item.description: An intimate experiment in writing beside two departed authors.

item.title: Art’s Generations
item.description: Inventing and reinventing the celebrated Dutch painter.

item.title: Murderous, Man-Hating, and Baby-Killing
item.description: Eleanor Johnson’s new book traces the lineage of the demonic women trope to its Mesopotamian origins.

item.title: Arcana Made Easy
item.description: Exploding notions of heteronormative occultist practice through reflections on two gallery exhibitions that celebrate queer arcana.

item.title: Revenge of a Church Lady
item.description: Deesha Philyaw’s debut novel is a high-stakes tale of morality, shame, and vulnerability.

item.title: Make Room in the Mouth
item.description: Two new collections of poetry look backward and forward at Indigenous history.

item.title: When Speaking Fails
item.description: Douglas Stuart’s new novel shows how unspoken secrets can ravage a family and a community.

item.title: Idyll Worship
item.description: Ukrainian author Khrystia Vengryniuk’s newly translated novel is a sly and disarming anti-pastoral about a province called America.
